questions.question: From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom. Labor of love.

options.text: A profuse or intense display or declaration of love or affection
An exclamation of surprise, shock, frustration, exasperation, anger, alarm, or annoyance
used to introduce some great sacrifice or demonstration of selfless goodwill
Work that is done for pleasure rather than money

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option (4)** i.e. **'Work that is done for pleasure rather than money'**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **'Labor of love'** refers to a task or piece of work that a person performs out of deep interest, passion, or personal satisfaction rather than for financial gain or external rewards. (मेहनत का वह काम जो खुशी के लिए किया जाए)
 
 
• **Example:** For the retired teacher, running a free library in his village is a **labor of love**.
 
 
 
• **'Work that is done for pleasure rather than money'** describes an activity undertaken primarily because the person enjoys doing it, without the expectation of being paid. (पैसे के बजाय खुशी के लिए किया गया काम)
 
 
• **Example:** Painting murals for the local orphanage is a **work that is done for pleasure rather than money** for her.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'Labor of love'** is **'Work that is done for pleasure rather than money'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is- **Work that is done for pleasure rather than money**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **A profuse or intense display or declaration of love or affection** (प्रेम या स्नेह का अत्यधिक प्रदर्शन): This refers to an abundant or very strong showing of emotional fondness towards someone.
 
 
• **Example:** His **profuse declaration of love** at the airport surprised everyone.
 
 
 
• **An exclamation of surprise, shock, frustration, exasperation, anger, alarm, or annoyance** (आश्चर्य, सदमा, क्रोध या झुंझलाहट की अभिव्यक्ति): This describes a sudden, loud cry or remark expressing a sharp emotional reaction.
 
 
• **Example:** 'Good grief!' is a common **exclamation of frustration** when things go wrong.
 
 
 
• **Used to introduce some great sacrifice or demonstration of selfless goodwill** (निस्वार्थ सद्भावना या बलिदान का प्रदर्शन): This phrase is used to highlight an act of altruism or kindness performed without selfish motives.
 
 
• **Example:** The soldier’s decision to stay behind was a final **demonstration of selfless goodwill** toward his comrades.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice? 

The storm destroyed many houses near the coast.

options.text: Many houses near the coast are destroyed by the storm.
Many houses near the coast were destroyed by the storm.
Many houses near the coast have been destroyed by the storm.
Many houses near the coast will be destroyed by the storm.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Many houses near the coast were destroyed by the storm**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence is in the **Active Voice** and follows the structure of the **Simple Past Tense**: **Subject + V2 (Past Tense Verb) + Object**.
 
• In the given sentence, **The storm** acts as the **Subject**, **destroyed** is the **Simple Past** form of the verb, and **many houses near the coast** is the **Object**.
 
• When converting a sentence from **Active** to **Passive Voice**, the **Object** of the active sentence becomes the **Subject** of the passive sentence.
 
• The standard formula for **Simple Past Tense** in the **Passive Voice** is: **New Subject + was/were + V3 (Past Participle) + by + New Object**.
 
• Since the new subject **Many houses near the coast** is **plural**, the auxiliary verb **were** must be used to maintain **Subject-Verb Agreement**.
 
• The **Past Participle** (V3) form of the verb **destroy** is **destroyed**, and the original subject **The storm** is added as the **agent** after the preposition **by**.
 
• Combining these elements, the correct passive sentence is: **Many houses near the coast were destroyed by the storm**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding **Tense Consistency** in **Voice Conversion**:
 
 
• **Simple Present Passive**: Formed using **is/am/are + V3**. It is used for habitual actions or general truths (e.g., **are destroyed**).
 
• **Present Perfect Passive**: Formed using **has/have + been + V3**. It indicates an action completed in the recent past with a connection to the present (e.g., **have been destroyed**).
 
• **Simple Future Passive**: Formed using **will + be + V3**. It is used for actions that are expected to happen in the future (e.g., **will be destroyed**).
 
• **Simple Past Passive**: Formed using **was/were + V3**. It must be used when the active verb is in the **Simple Past** to preserve the original meaning.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice? 

The latest safety regulations are being strictly implemented by the transport department.

options.text: The transport department strictly implements the latest safety regulations.
The transport department is strictly implementing the latest safety regulations.
The transport department strictly implemented the latest safety regulations.
The transport department has strictly implemented the latest safety regulations.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The transport department is strictly implementing the latest safety regulations.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice** of the **Present Continuous Tense**, as indicated by the structure **are being + past participle (implemented)**.
 
• When converting from **Passive to Active Voice**, the object of the preposition 'by' (**the transport department**) becomes the **subject** of the active sentence.
 
• In the **Present Continuous Tense**, the active voice construction follows the pattern: **Subject + is/am/are + present participle (verb + ing) + Object**.
 
• The subject **the transport department** is a singular entity, necessitating the use of the singular auxiliary verb **is** followed by the main verb **implementing**.
 
• The original subject of the passive sentence (**the latest safety regulations**) shifts to the **object position** in the active sentence.
 
• The adverb **strictly** maintains its position to modify the verb, resulting in the correct active form: **is strictly implementing**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding **Tense Consistency** during voice conversion:
 
 
• **Simple Present**: If the active verb is **implements**, the passive is **is/are implemented**.
 
• **Present Continuous**: If the active verb is **is implementing**, the passive is **is/are being implemented**.
 
• **Simple Past**: If the active verb is **implemented**, the passive is **was/were implemented**.
 
• **Present Perfect**: If the active verb is **has implemented**, the passive is **has/have been implemented**.
 
 
 
• The **Active Voice** is generally preferred in professional and clear communication as it identifies the **doer of the action** directly and is typically more concise than the **Passive Voice**.
</ul

which has to be addressed immediately.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error in the sentence is the incorrect use of the preposition **of** in **Part 3**.
 
• When discussing a specific functional or mechanical fault within a machine, device, or system, the preposition **with** is idiomatically correct.
 
• The phrase **problem of** is typically reserved for defining the nature of an abstract issue or a general situation (e.g., the **problem of** poverty).
 
• To indicate a malfunction in a component, the sentence should correctly use **problem with the ignition system**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'There is an irreparable **problem with the ignition system** of the car, which has to be addressed immediately.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Part 1: 'There is an'** – This is grammatically sound. The indefinite article **an** correctly precedes the word **irreparable**, which begins with a vowel sound.
 
• **Part 2: 'irreparable problem'** – The adjective **irreparable** is used correctly to describe a problem that cannot be repaired or rectified.
 
• **Part 4: 'which has to be addressed immediately'** – This relative clause is grammatically correct and appropriately conveys the necessity of urgent action.
</ul

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. She was a beautiful baby.
A. You did not know her all those years she was thought homely, or see her poring over her baby pictures, making me tell her over and over how beautiful she had been - and would be, I would tell her - and was now, to the seeing eye.
B. But the seeing eyes were few or non-existent.
C. The first and only one of our five that was beautiful at birth.
D. You do not guess how new and uneasy her tenancy in her now-loveliness.
S2. Including mine.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph describes the life and changing appearance of a girl, moving from her birth to her present state. 
• **Sentence S1 is the starting point**, establishing that she was a **beautiful baby**. 
• **Sentence C follows immediately** as it adds specific detail to the claim in S1: 
• 'The first and only one of our **five** that was **beautiful at birth**.' 
• **Sentence D is the second sentence** because it shifts the focus from her birth to her present situation, describing her current beauty as a **new and uneasy tenancy**: 
• 'You do not guess how new and uneasy her tenancy in her **now-loveliness**.' 
• **Sentence A follows** by explaining the long interval between her birth and her current beauty, mentioning the years she was **thought homely** and introducing the term **seeing eye**: 
• 'You did not know her all those years she was thought homely... and was now, to the **seeing eye**.' 
• **Sentence B is the fourth sentence** as it directly responds to the phrase 'seeing eye' from the end of sentence A: 
• 'But the **seeing eyes** were **few or non-existent**.' 
• **Sentence S2 concludes** the paragraph by adding a final qualifying detail to sentence B: 
• '**Including mine**.' 
• The logically coherent sequence is **CDAB**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'She was a **beautiful baby**. The first and only one of our **five** that was **beautiful at birth**. You do not guess how new and uneasy her tenancy in her **now-loveliness**. You did not know her all those years she was **thought homely**, or see her poring over her baby pictures, making me tell her over and over how beautiful she had been - and would be, I would tell her - and was now, to the **seeing eye**. But the **seeing eyes** were **few or non-existent**. **Including mine**.'</div

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

• The paragraph describes a past encounter with a woman whom the narrator remembers through a specific detail: a ring.

• **S1 is the fixed starting sentence**, which introduces the mystery of the woman and the significance of a **ring** on her right forefinger.

• **Sentence D is the second sentence** as it initiates the flashback, providing the setting and time of their first meeting: **thirty-four years earlier in Vienna** at a tavern for Latin American students.

• **Sentence A is the third sentence** because it adds specific descriptive details about that day in Vienna. It mentions the narrator's arrival from **Rome** and specifically identifies the **Egyptian ring in the shape of a serpent**, which directly connects back to the ring mentioned in **S1**.

• **Sentence C is the fourth sentence** as it moves from her appearance to her speech and the narrator's assumption about her identity. Because she spoke **elementary Spanish** in a **metallic accent**, the narrator **thought she was the only Austrian** at the table.

• **Sentence B is the fifth sentence** because it uses the contrastive phrase '**But no**' to correct the assumption made in sentence C. It reveals her true origin as being **born in Colombia** and explains her presence in **Austria** to study **music and voice**.

• **S2 is the fixed closing sentence**, which concludes the description of her during that period, noting she was **about thirty** and had **begun to age before her time**.

• The correct logical sequence is **DACB**.

I had come from Rome that morning, and I still remember my immediate response to her splendid soprano's bosom, the languid foxtails on her coat collar, and that Egyptian ring in the shape of a serpent. She spoke an elementary Spanish in a metallic accent without pausing for breath, and I thought she was the only Austrian at the long wooden table. But no, she had been born in Colombia and had come to Austria between the wars, when she was little more than a child, to study music and voice. She was about thirty, and did not carry her years well, for she had never been pretty and had begun to age before her time.'

 

Therefore, the correct sequence is **Option 1 (DACB)**.</div

questions.question: A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required." The students worked hard and were thus able to complete the assignment on time.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence **'The students worked hard...'** is grammatically correct and logically sound.
 
• In this context, **'hard'** functions as an **adverb** meaning 'with a great deal of effort' or 'intensely.'
 
• The adverb **'hard'** correctly modifies the verb **'worked,'** explaining how the students performed the action to achieve the result of completing the assignment.
 
• Since the sentence is already correct in its structure and meaning, **no improvement** is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is **4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The students **worked hard** and were thus able to complete the assignment on time.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 'worked hardly'** – The word **'hardly'** is an adverb that means 'scarcely' or 'almost not.' If used, it would mean the students did almost no work, which contradicts their ability to finish the assignment.
 
• **Option 2: 'worked very harder'** – This is grammatically incorrect. The adverb **'very'** cannot be used to modify the **comparative degree** ('harder'). One would instead use 'much harder' or 'even harder.'
 
• **Option 3: 'worked hardest'** – This is the **superlative degree**. It is generally used when comparing the effort of one group against two or more other groups. In a simple descriptive sentence like this, the **positive degree** ('hard') is the standard choice.
</ul

questions.question: What is the main moral lesson Chaucer shares in The Pardoner's Tale?

questions.solution:

__

• The text explicitly states that the author uses this story to communicate the message: '**Greed is the root of all evil**.'
 
• The narrative describes three **drunken revelers** who discover a **treasure** and, driven by their **greed**, kill each other to gain sole possession of the gold.
 
• This tragic ending serves as a direct illustration of how the desire for wealth leads to **moral corruption** and **death**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Exemplum:** A story used in discourse to illustrate a **moral** or **thematic** point, which was highly popular during the **Middle Ages**.
 
• The characters in the tale originally set out to confront **Death**, but their own **greed** becomes the instrument through which they eventually meet him.
 
• While other virtues like **honesty** or **loyalty** are important in literature, the passage specifically focuses on **greed** as the central theme of this particular tale.
 
• **Chaucer** is noted for using multiple **exempla** across his works, such as in **The Nun's Priest's Tale**, where **Chanticleer** presents ten examples to argue about the significance of **dreams**.
</ul
